name: Kinesiology / face taping

card.summary: Elastic sports tape applied to the face to 'retrain' muscles; the tape's general evidence is limited and facial use is untested.
card.aka: face taping, Kinesio tape on face
card.note: No studies of cosmetic facial use found; adhesive effects on facial skin not documented in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Face taping borrows elastic kinesiology tape from sports medicine and applies it to the face, with the claimed aim of retraining muscles or holding tissue.

Reviews of the tape for musculoskeletal pain and strength report small or inconsistent effects, and no study of cosmetic facial use was found.
quick.mechanism: Manufacturers say the tape supports tissue, aids lymph drainage and improves proprioception. Critics and some researchers say these mechanisms are unsupported and benefits may reflect placebo.
quick.risks: Safety for facial use is not documented in the sources reviewed. Adhesive tape in general can irritate skin.

lead: Kinesiology or face taping is the application of elastic therapeutic tape, of the kind developed for sports and musculoskeletal use, to the face. In appearance-focused communities it is used with the aim of looking more lifted and less puffy: people tape to hold facial tissue in a supported position, to retrain facial muscles, or to reduce puffiness and under-eye shadows.[1][3]

The idea is discussed in a looksmax.org thread titled as a question about whether face taping could be the next looksmax. The author argues that facial skin sags with gravity and sleep loss, and that gentle mechanical tension or compression from tape might change how skin and underlying fat behave. Commenters extend the idea to mouth taping, saying it could reduce lower-face bloat and under-eye circles.[3] These are community theories rather than findings.

Elastic kinesiology tape was developed in the 1970s by Kenzo Kase, a Japanese-American chiropractor, and is sold under the Kinesio brand among others. Manufacturers have claimed benefits for muscle support, lymphatic drainage, pain signalling and proprioception; published reviews in musculoskeletal conditions report small or inconsistent effects, and some researchers attribute reported benefits to placebo.[1] No published study has tested kinesiology tape for cosmetic facial purposes. A registered trial compares a physiotherapy technique with kinesiology taping in patients with Bell's palsy, a medical condition.[2]

chain: Elastic tape is applied to areas of the face
Tape holds or gently compresses tissue and is said to encourage lymph movement
Practitioners hope for a lifted, less puffy look
angle.text: People who tape their faces do it to hold tissue in a lifted position and to reduce morning puffiness, borrowing the lymph-drainage and muscle-support rationale used for sports tape. Forum users also propose that mechanical tension could, over time, reshape how skin and fat behave. These effects are described by users and manufacturers rather than measured on the face.

infobox: Stretchy cotton with heat-activated acrylic adhesive[1]
Up to about four days (body use)[1]

paras: Kinesiology tape is a thin, stretchy, latex-free cotton strip that can stretch to roughly 140% of its length and bonds with a heat-activated acrylic adhesive. On the body it may be worn for several days.[1]

Facial taping adapts the sports technique to the cheeks, jawline, forehead or around the eyes, with the aim of a lifted, smoother look. In the looksmax.org discussion, the author reasons that skin stretches downward with gravity during the day and recovers during sleep, and speculates that sustained stretch thins the fat layer while compression thickens it, citing a paper on mechanical regulation of adipose tissue volume.[3] A reply suggests the same logic could extend to the scalp and hair.[3]

A related practice is mouth taping, in which a strip of surgical tape holds the lips closed during sleep. Wikipedia reports that it became a social media trend in the 2020s, that its health claims have not been scientifically verified, and that small studies have examined snoring and sleep apnea; it does not describe facial appearance effects.[4] Forum users nonetheless claim it affects lower-face bloat and under-eye circles.[3]

Manufacturers state that the tape supports muscles, tendons, ligaments and joints, and further claims include improved lymphatic drainage, reduced pain signalling and better proprioception. Critics say these claims lack supporting evidence.[1]

A 2012 meta-analysis reported trivial pain relief and little quality evidence for the tape over other elastic taping in sports injuries. A 2014 meta-analysis reported negligible effects on muscle strength, with lower-quality studies more likely to report benefit. A 2015 meta-analysis found the tape outperformed no treatment for chronic musculoskeletal pain but not other treatments, and did not reduce disability. A 2018 study found tape colour, placement and tension did not measurably affect performance, strength or function. Some researchers attribute reported benefits to a placebo effect.[1] More recent trials and reviews continue to examine taping for ankle instability, shoulder pain and plantar fasciitis.[5][6]
Safety of taping facial skin has not been studied. Adhesive tape in general can irritate skin, and the Kinesio tape article describes the product as bonded with an acrylic adhesive.[1]

No studies found for cosmetic facial taping. One registered trial in Bell's palsy patients compares Kabat rehabilitation with kinesiology taping; it was listed as active, not recruiting, with 38 participants, and no results were reviewed.[2] Studies of the tape in other body regions include a 2022 meta-analysis in athletes with chronic ankle instability and a randomised trial in plantar fasciitis.[5][6]

timeline.event: Kenzo Kase develops elastic kinesiology tape.[1]
Meta-analyses report small or inconsistent effects in musculoskeletal conditions.[1]
Mouth taping spreads on social media.[4]

lore.intro: Face taping appears on looksmax.org as an experimental idea framed around gravity, sleep and skin tension, alongside mouth taping.[3]

claims.claim: Taping the face counters gravity-driven sagging and holds a lifted look.
claims.believers: The thread author argues facial skin stretches downward over the day and that tape could counter this tension.[3]
claims.experts: No published study has tested kinesiology tape on facial skin; reviews of the tape elsewhere in the body report small or inconsistent effects.[1]

claims.claim: Mouth taping reduces lower-face bloat and under-eye circles.
claims.believers: A commenter in the thread says it removes lower-face bloat, adds fullness to the upper face and reduces under-eye circles.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that health claims for mouth taping are unverified, with a few small studies on snoring and sleep apnea and none on facial appearance.[4]

claims.claim: Sustained skin stretch or compression changes the fat layer under the skin.
claims.believers: The author cites research on mechanical regulation of adipose tissue volume to suggest stretch thins and compression thickens fat.[3]
claims.experts: That research is not about facial tape, and no study links taping to facial fat changes.
